lines: Some words are everywhere. Movie appears in every movie review.
A word that is everywhere tells us nothing. TF-IDF gives it a small weight.
Movie is in all four reviews, so its weight becomes zero.
Good is only in two, so it keeps its weight. Rare words count more.
One important rule.
The test set is the model's final exam. The model must not see it before.
So learn the vocabulary and the weights from the training set only.
Then only apply them to the test set. Otherwise the test leaks into training.
Counting words loses the order. So neural models read the text word by word.
A recurrent network, an RNN, carries a memory from one word to the next.
But in a long sentence, the early words fade away. This is the vanishing gradient problem.
An LSTM adds gates. They decide what to keep, what to write, and what to show. So it remembers longer.
The transformer takes another way: attention.
Every word looks at every other word directly, all at the same time.
In: the animal was tired because it, the word it looks most at animal.
BERT is a big transformer trained on lots of text first. Then we add a small head and fine-tune it for our task.
How do we measure a classifier?
Precision: of everything we flagged, how much was right?
Recall: of everything that was really there, how much did we find?
F1 combines the two into one number.
For the exam:
TF-IDF makes common words weak.
Fit on the training set only.
RNN, then LSTM, then attention: each one keeps more of the sentence.
Precision is about your alarms. Recall is about what you missed.
